name: Semax
used_for: A synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide derived from an ACTH fragment, developed in Russia. A secondary source (an encyclopedia page, not an official register) says it is on Russia's list of vital and essential drugs and is used there for conditions such as stroke; the same source says it is not FDA approved in the US. It is promoted online as a focus and memory aid. The human evidence found is small and Russian, with one non-placebo-controlled stroke-rehabilitation study; most other work is in rodents and cell models.

entries.text: Two courses of 6000 mcg per day for 10 days each, with a 20-day gap, were given in a stroke rehabilitation study (administration route not stated in the abstract). The study was not placebo-controlled.

internet_entries.text: A peptide-tracking app's blog (Regimen) says standard nasal Semax use is described in tiers: 100 mcg per nostril once daily at the low end, 200 to 300 mcg per nostril per session once or twice daily as a standard level, and 600 to 1,000 mcg per day split across two to three sessions at the high end. This is the source's description, not a recommendation.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

internet_entries.text: An educational dosing-guide website (DosingCalc) says a commonly described starting amount is 300 mcg per nostril once daily (600 mcg total), with 450 mcg per nostril (900 mcg total) described as a later level, a split option of 300 mcg twice daily, and up to 1,200 mcg per day in short intensive use. These are the source's statements, not established or recommended doses.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: In a trial of 110 people after ischemic stroke, the standard Semax regimen was two courses of 10 days each, separated by a 20-day interval. The abstract does not state the route of administration.
administration_guidance.label: research

administration_guidance.text: A prescribing clinic's guide (Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center) says Semax is usually dosed in the morning and early afternoon, with late-day use avoided to prevent sleep interference, that intranasal is the most common route, and that a reconstituted vial is kept refrigerated and used within a few weeks.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: A peptide information site (The Peptide Initiative, which states it sells no products) describes three routes for Semax (intranasal as the preferred one, or subcutaneous injection in the abdomen or outer thigh with sites rotated), says it can be used regardless of food, and says different nasal peptides are spaced 15 to 30 minutes apart.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: A prescribing clinic's guide (Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center) lists nasal irritation, dryness or sting, mild headache, lightheadedness and fatigue as reported effects of Semax, plus overstimulation or sleep trouble when used late in the day, and notes long-term effects are unknown given limited human data.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A Superpower guide says Semax is a Russian-developed peptide that may raise BDNF and NGF and may help stroke recovery and cognition, but notes the largest human study (110 stroke patients) was non-randomized and not placebo-controlled, and that it is not FDA approved.
Swolverine, a supplement retailer's blog, presents Semax as a focus-enhancing peptide that raises BDNF and cites Russian clinical data as support; the page is informational and does not sell Semax.

Nuusflits says Semax and Selank remain registered drugs in Russia but that the FDA has never reviewed them, and says FDA moved them to Category 1 for compounding in February 2026. The FDA page consulted instead lists them as nominated but withdrawn, so this claim could not be confirmed.

research.summary: Russian study (Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova) of 110 patients after ischemic stroke, split by early or late rehabilitation and by whether they received Semax. Not randomized or placebo-controlled as described.
research.finding: Patients given Semax had higher blood BDNF levels and the authors report faster functional recovery on the Barthel index and better motor performance. Because groups were not placebo-controlled, this cannot show that Semax caused the improvement.

research.summary: Small brain-imaging study (Dokl Biol Sci) comparing resting-state fMRI connectivity before and after an injection of Semax, Selank or placebo in volunteers.
research.finding: Differences in connectivity between the right amygdala and right temporal regions were found after Semax and Selank. This is a brain-activity measure, not evidence of a clinical benefit.

research.summary: Rat study (Neuropeptides) of whether Semax could reverse behavioral and brain chemistry changes caused by early-life exposure to the antidepressant fluvoxamine.
research.finding: Semax reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved maze learning and normalized brain monoamine levels in the rats. Rat results do not establish effects in people.

research.summary: Mouse and cell study (Br J Pharmacol) of Semax after spinal cord injury in female mice, plus a PC12 cell model.
research.finding: Semax improved functional recovery in the injured mice and reduced markers of cell death in the models; the authors link this to the mu-opioid receptor. Animal and cell evidence only.

research.summary: Laboratory study (ACS Chem Neurosci) of Semax in artificial membrane models with amyloid beta and copper.
research.finding: Semax reduced copper-driven amyloid beta aggregation and related toxicity in test-tube models. It is not evidence for any effect in Alzheimer's disease in people.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances nominated for compounding that may present significant safety risks (page dated 04/22/2026, fetched 2026-09-30).
research.finding: The page lists Semax among substances nominated but withdrawn (not in the active Category 2 list), with this FDA statement: "Compounded drugs containing semax (heptapeptide) may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities." The page does not make it an approved drug.

research.summary: Russian clinical and electrophysiological study (Gusev et al., Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova) of 30 patients in the acute phase of ischemic stroke given Semax, compared with 80 patients with similar strokes who had conventional treatment only. Not randomized as described, and the abstract does not state the route.
research.finding: Adding Semax was linked to faster regress of general brain and especially motor deficits. The authors report the most effective daily doses were 12 mg for moderate strokes and 18 mg for severe strokes, over treatment courses of 5 and 10 days.

research.summary: Russian study (Gusev et al., Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova) of 187 patients with different stages of cerebrovascular insufficiency (reduced blood flow to the brain) treated with Semax. The abstract does not describe a control group, dose or route.
research.finding: The authors report clinical improvement, stabilization of disease progress, fewer strokes and transient ischemic attacks, and a minor percentage of side effects with good tolerability, including in older patients.

research.summary: Russian retrospective comparative analysis (Miasoedova et al., Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova) of immune and biochemical markers in patients with acute ischemic stroke given Semax.
research.finding: The authors report a shift toward anti-inflammatory markers (interleukin-10, tumor necrosis factor-alpha) over markers that maintain inflammation (interleukin-8, C-reactive protein). It is a retrospective analysis, so it cannot prove cause.

dose.summary: Studied doses in Russian stroke trials were 6 mg a day (two 10-day courses) and 12 to 18 mg a day for 5 to 10 days; the route is not stated in the abstracts. Online sources describe 100 to 1,200 mcg a day as a nasal spray and about 250 mcg to 1 mg per injection under the skin, none of it tested.

items.text: Two courses of 6,000 mcg per day for 10 days each, with a 20-day gap, were given to 110 adults after ischemic stroke. The study had comparison groups but was not randomized or placebo-controlled, and the abstract does not state the route.
items.label: research

items.text: In a Russian study of 30 patients in the acute phase of ischemic stroke, the authors report the most effective daily doses were 12 mg for moderate strokes and 18 mg for severe strokes. The abstract does not state the route.
items.label: research

items.text: In a study of 52 healthy volunteers, Semax was given as an injection (type and dose not stated in the abstract) and brain scans were done 5 and 20 minutes later. This shows a single injection was given to healthy people, but gives no usable dose.
items.label: research

items.text: Regimen, a peptide-tracking app's blog, describes nasal Semax in tiers: 100 mcg per nostril once daily at the low end, 200 to 300 mcg per nostril per session once or twice daily as standard, and 600 to 1,000 mcg per day split over two to three sessions at the high end. It also says injection under the skin runs 500 mcg to 1 mg once daily.
items.label: internet

items.text: DosingCalc, an educational dosing-guide site, says a commonly described start is 300 mcg per nostril once daily, with 450 mcg per nostril as a later level, a split option of 300 mcg twice daily, and up to 1,200 mcg per day in short intensive use. It says only community protocols, not published trials, give these numbers.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative, an educational peptide site, describes 250 to 500 mcg per day in weeks 1 and 2, then 500 to 900 mcg per day in weeks 3 and 4, with nasal spray as the preferred route and injection under the skin as an alternative.
items.label: internet

items.text: Swolverine, a supplement retailer's blog, says a 0.1% solution is used as 1 to 2 drops per nostril twice daily, and that a stronger 1% form exists for stroke use.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptidepedia says a standard dose is 200 to 600 mcg once or twice daily, and that the nasal route is preferred with injection under the skin as an alternative.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, says typical nasal use is 200 to 600 mcg per day, and that injection under the skin is described at 250 to 600 mcg per dose.
items.label: internet

items.text: FormBlends, a compounded-peptide seller, says typical intranasal doses are 250 to 600 mcg per day, starting at 250 mcg, and that its article covers the nasal spray only.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, says nasal use is about 0.6 to 1.5 mg per day in two doses and that injection under the skin has sparse human data.
items.label: internet

timing.summary: Trials do not report time of day. Online sources say morning and early afternoon, and to avoid late-day doses that may disturb sleep; this is untested.

items.text: In a study of 52 healthy volunteers, brain scans 5 and 20 minutes after an injection of Semax showed changes in connectivity between the right amygdala and temporal brain regions. This measures brain activity soon after dosing, not a benefit.
items.label: research

items.text: Regimen says to take Semax in the morning and early afternoon only, not after 3 to 4 PM because it may disturb sleep, ideally 15 to 30 minutes before a hard focus block. It says effects appear in 5 to 15 minutes after nasal use.
items.label: internet

items.text: DosingCalc says only community protocols specify morning dosing and that published trials do not document time of day.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says the best time is morning (7 to 10 AM), with any second dose before 2 PM.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptidepedia says to take Semax in the morning or early afternoon and that late-day use interferes with sleep.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, says Semax is usually dosed in the morning and early afternoon, with late-day use avoided to prevent sleep interference.
items.label: internet

items.text: FormBlends, a compounded-peptide seller, says to take the first dose within an hour of waking, a second dose between mid-morning and early afternoon, and nothing after 2 to 3 PM.
items.label: internet

fasting.summary: No trial or label rule on food was found. One educational site says it can be used regardless of food; other sources say nothing.

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says Semax can be taken regardless of food because it is used nasally and absorbs directly into the brain tissue. This claim is untested.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: The Russian stroke trials gave it daily in short courses. Online sources describe once to three times daily, and some describe weekdays on and weekends off; none of this is tested.

items.text: In the 110-patient stroke trial, the same daily dose was given for 10 days in each course. The 30-patient acute stroke study gave daily doses for 5 or 10 days.
items.label: research

items.text: Regimen describes sessions once or twice daily as standard and up to two to three sessions at the high end, and says a popular schedule is 5 days on and 2 days off (weekdays on, weekends off) to keep receptors sensitive. This reasoning is untested.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says it is dosed once to twice daily because effects on brain growth factors are said to last 12 to 24 hours, and that different nasal peptides are spaced 15 to 30 minutes apart.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, says doses are commonly split between morning and midday, and that injections under the skin are described once daily or a few times a week.
items.label: internet

items.text: FormBlends, a compounded-peptide seller, says to space doses 4 to 6 hours apart.
items.label: internet

cycle_length.summary: The studied courses were 10 days, repeated once after a 20-day gap, and 5 to 10 days in acute stroke. Online sources describe 10 to 14 day courses up to 4 to 8 weeks with breaks; no study tested these cycles.

items.text: In the 110-patient stroke trial, two 10-day courses were separated by a 20-day gap, with outcomes followed for about 5 months. BDNF in blood stayed higher in the Semax groups through the follow-up. It was not placebo-controlled.
items.label: research

items.text: In the 30-patient acute stroke study, treatment courses were 5 days for moderate strokes and 10 days for severe strokes.
items.label: research

items.text: Regimen describes 3 weeks on and 1 week off as a popular cycle.
items.label: internet

items.text: DosingCalc says community practice is 10 to 14 days on and 7 to 10 days off, with no published source, and that no long-term safety study in healthy users was found.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptidepedia says courses run 10 to 30 days with breaks of 2 to 4 weeks.
items.label: internet

items.text: Swolverine says a 0.1% solution is used for 10 to 16 days.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, says a course is 2 to 4 weeks, followed by a break, with no endless daily use.
items.label: internet

items.text: FormBlends, a compounded-peptide seller, says Russian protocols use 10 to 14 day courses and Western practice is 4 to 8 weeks on, then 2 to 4 weeks off.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, describes a 10 to 14 day short course, a 4 to 6 week extended course, and 4 to 6 weeks on with 2 to 4 weeks off.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: No label or stability study was found. Online sources say to refrigerate sprays and mixed vials for weeks; one notes no stability study exists. For injection, sources describe the abdomen or outer thigh.

items.text: Regimen says an opened pre-made spray is best refrigerated, with room temperature acceptable short term, for 1 to 3 months. A solution mixed at home is refrigerated at 2 to 8 C for up to 28 days. Bottles are kept upright, away from sun and heat.
items.label: internet

items.text: DosingCalc says refrigeration at 2 to 8 C is general practice for mixed peptides, but found no published stability study for Semax mixed in bacteriostatic water.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says powder is kept refrigerated or frozen, and a mixed solution is kept in the refrigerator at 36 to 46 F, never frozen, for 30 days.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative describes injection under the skin of the abdomen (2 inches from the navel, rotating sides) or the middle third of the outer thigh.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, says adding 2 mL of bacteriostatic water to a 10 mg vial gives 5 mg per mL, and that a mixed vial is kept refrigerated and used within a few weeks.
items.label: internet

items.text: FormBlends, a compounded-peptide seller, says compounded Semax nasal solution goes in the fridge, to follow the label's use-by date, and that brief room temperature use is fine.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Dosing Protocols, a site with supplier affiliate links, says powder vials go in the freezer long term or the fridge short term, and a mixed solution is refrigerated and used within several weeks.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: How it works in people is not known. Animal and lab work point to brain growth factors, immune genes and opioid or melanocortin receptors.

items.text: A rat study found Semax reduced anxiety-like behavior and normalized brain monoamine levels (chemical messengers such as serotonin) after early-life antidepressant exposure. Animal evidence only.
items.label: research

items.text: In mice with spinal cord injury, Semax improved recovery, and the authors link this to the mu-opioid receptor. Animal and cell evidence only.
items.label: research

items.text: In patients with acute ischemic stroke, a retrospective analysis reported a shift toward anti-inflammatory markers after Semax. It cannot prove cause.
items.label: research

items.text: In the 110-patient stroke study, blood levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) were higher in patients given Semax. The study was not placebo-controlled.
items.label: research

items.text: Wikipedia says the mechanism of action of Semax is unknown, though it may involve melanocortin receptors or enzymes that break down enkephalins.
items.label: internet

items.text: Superpower, a health testing company's guide, says Semax binds melanocortin receptors and raises BDNF and nerve growth factor (NGF) in the hippocampus and cortex, citing a rat result of up to 1.4-fold more BDNF.
items.label: internet

items.text: Swolverine, a supplement retailer's blog, says Semax raises BDNF and its receptor TrkB and tunes dopamine and serotonin.
items.label: internet

best_documented_effect.summary: Small Russian stroke studies report faster recovery, but they were not placebo-controlled, so the benefit is unproven. Online sources promote focus and memory.

items.text: In 110 adults after ischemic stroke, those given Semax had higher blood BDNF and faster gains on the Barthel index (a daily-living score) and motor scale. Groups were not placebo-controlled or randomized.
items.label: research

items.text: In 30 patients in the acute phase of stroke compared with 80 patients on usual care, adding Semax was linked to faster recovery of motor deficits.
items.label: research

items.text: In 187 patients with cerebrovascular insufficiency, the authors report clinical improvement and fewer strokes. The abstract does not describe a control group.
items.label: research

items.text: Superpower, a health testing company's guide, says Semax may help stroke recovery and cognition, but notes the largest human study (110 stroke patients) was non-randomized and not placebo-controlled.
items.label: internet

items.text: Swolverine, a supplement retailer's blog, says Russian clinical data show it sharpened attention and short-term memory, most under fatigue. No source study is named in the page.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Common
side_effect_groups.summary: Trials report few side effects. Online sources list nasal irritation, headache, restlessness and trouble sleeping.

items.text: In 187 patients with cerebrovascular insufficiency, the authors report a minor percentage of side effects and good tolerability, including in older patients. Details were not in the abstract.
items.label: research

items.text: Regimen lists occasional nasal irritation and dryness, rare headache, occasional restlessness and insomnia from late dosing, and calls it one of the mildest peptides.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says the Russian prescribing label lists mild irritation of the nasal lining with prolonged use as the main adverse effect. It could not be checked against the label here.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, lists nasal irritation, dryness or sting, mild headache, lightheadedness and fatigue, plus overstimulation or sleep trouble when used late or too high, and rare allergic reactions.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Long-term safety
side_effect_groups.summary: No long-term safety study in healthy people was found.

items.text: DosingCalc says no negative effects were reported in a developers' review but found no long-term safety study in healthy users.
items.label: internet

items.text: Beverly Hills Rejuvenation Center, a clinic that offers peptide programs, notes long-term effects are unknown given limited human data.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Regulator warning
side_effect_groups.summary: FDA says compounded Semax may cause immune reactions from clumping or impurities. Semax is approved only in Russia.

items.text: FDA lists Semax among substances nominated for compounding and then withdrawn, stating compounded Semax may pose immunogenicity risk for certain routes of administration due to potential aggregation and peptide-related impurities.
items.label: research

items.text: Nuusflits says Semax remains registered in Russia, that the FDA has never reviewed it, and that FDA moved it to Category 1 for compounding in February 2026. The FDA page checked lists it as nominated but withdrawn, so the Category 1 claim could not be confirmed.
items.label: internet
